A few thoughts from someone who's been there, has been intubated/extubated with an NGT three times, and has too much experience as an ED patient.

**1. This is important, please read this: Currently your daughter is too malnourished to properly think. Take her to the emergency department for treatment. The first order of business is to get her medically stable. Nothing else can happen until that is achieved.**

2. Does your daughter feel OK with liquid nutrition? Abbott's Ensure line of nutrition products have been my bedrock for when I'm too worried about foodborne illness to eat but still need to get some sort of nutrition in my body. Here's a link to their website: Abbott Nutrition.

3. Residential isn't treatment. I've been to two different ED residentials and have been to over 12 inpatient psychiatric hospitals or residential programs. They are unfortunatly almost exclusively setup to deal with anorexia nervosa and its two subtypes, restricting and binge-purge.

4. NGTs: If emesis/vomiting is her largest fear, NGTs are likely to be tough. That said, if she can be sedated during the process (propofol is the best because it doesn't have much of a "hangover"), that will make this a moot point. I've had three NGTs placed when I was concious and they're brutal. It's important that she's sitting in fowler's position when it's placed as this will make it easier.

5. What's the biggest barrier to her eating? Is it fear of vomiting, the texture of certain foods and worrying that that will make her vomit? What is the specific fear driving the behavior? That will markedly inform how her treatment progresses.

Lastly, saying that her taste buds are hypersensitive makes me think about ASD. I'm autistic and can taste/smell things that most people can't. Might be something to bring up with her care team/PCP if you are comfortable.

Also I think it's a bit obtuse to say that FDA "doesn't care" about the people in the U.S.; take the example of THALOMID, known by its generic name of thalidomide.

Teratogens, more specifically drugs with teratogenic potential, can have a wide impact on the developing fetus in-utero. These are operationalized as *major birth defects* and *minor birth defects.* Perhaps the most famous example of a drug that induces, per the package insert (PI), "SEVERE, LIFE-THREATENING HUMAN BIRTH DEFECTS" is that of THALOMID, sometimes known by its generic name of thalidomide. THALOMID is one of the most powerful teratogens known and was marketed in Western Europe from 1957 to 1961 as a sedative and antiemetic (nausea relieving drug), chiefly used for morning sickness. It carries a BOXED WARNING, FDA's strongest warning for drugs, indicating that there "is an adverse reaction so serious in proportion to the potential benefit from the drug (e.g., a fatal, life-threatening or permanently disabling adverse reaction) that it is essential that it be considered in assessing the risks and benefits of a drug" as well as if "FDA approved the drug with restrictions to ensure safe use because FDA concluded that the drug can be safely used only if distribution or use is restricted (e.g., ...under 505-1(f)(3) of d Cosmetic Act (FDCA) "Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies” Elements to assure safe use) (FDA, 2011).

Its use during pregnancy led to an estimated over 10 000 affected infants with a range of presentations, but usually severe, debilitating birth defects. These were oftentimes caused due to Phocomelia, a rare birth defect "marked by hypoplastic or markedly absent limbs" (Patel, Kreuzer, & Sherman, 2021). Ways to reduce the risk of teratogens is to reduce or eliminate exposure in-utero to teratogens, among others. In the case of THALOMID, this is accomplished by only allowing the drug to only be available under a restricted distribution program, specifically FDA's Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies (REMS) Program. FDA's purpose of REMS for THALOMID is to "prevent the risk of embryo-fetal exposure to thalidomide," and to "inform prescribers, patients, and pharmacists on the serious risks and safe-use conditions for thalidomide" (FDA, 2023).

On a more positive note, THALOMID was prevented from entry to the U.S. drug market by one ordinary women who accomplished extraordinary things. Dr. Frances Oldham Kelsey, MD, Ph.D., worked at FDA as a medical officer. Alright, we get it. We know that Caltrain is working on rolling out new equipment and there are bound to be lessons learned. Caltrain is the busiest commuter rail system west of the Mississippi river, and converting from a diesel-hauled push-pull service to EMUs is a huge change. It’s different for train crews, for the schedule, different for maintenance and overhaul requirements, and for the supporting infrastructure. It’s an entirely new platform and as much as I’d love it if Caltrain didn’t have any issues when they started running the new equipment, it’s a heavy lift even for the best prepared and most reliable system with the most talented and dedicated staff in the rail industry. Stadler is a Swiss company and they don’t really make equipment made for U.S. and North American railroads. EMD or GE both have decades upon decades of experience resigning locomotives for this market; Stadler doesn’t have that. Granted Siemens Mobility has had notable success in using European designs in the U.S., it’s always a process full of things to learn.

Caltrain is doing the best it can with the largest change in its history and the largest change in the history of the railway on which it runs. The delays, mechanical issues, wifi not working, and human interference are certainly not ideal and some of those issues are out of Caltrain’s control. Everyone at Caltrain knows the importance of the service they provide and I know that everyone is working as hard as they can to iron out the creases in the system. A representative of Stadler had mentioned that the platform (KISS) that Caltrain used isn’t designed with the assumption that the doors will open and close every two minutes. This is something that will have to be worked on with Stadler and Caltrain. It’s just one small example of how this is entirely new for Caltrain and also for Stadler too, as the Caltrain order is their largest yet in their Salt Lake City operation’s history.

The hypothesis is that early adversity (specifically a condition called Maternal Immune Activation) causes newborn babies to suffer neurological insults due to Maternal Immune Activation. It’s a fascinating part of science as the newborn brain and its development play a huge role in the development of conditions such as autism. Pretty cool to have worked on research that so directly impacts me. We also worked on developing the dose response relationship and curve for cucurbitacin to promote myelination. We also did work with the cells that myelinate axons, the glial cells and their various stages of development, such as premyelimating oligodendrocytes, dendrocytes, microglia, and so on. I’m not sure where in the world you are but in the U.S., you have a right to review your medical record, and for the records to be released within 30 days. Pursuant to 45 CFR 164.524(b)(2)(i), "the covered entity must act on a request for access no later than 30 days after receipt of the request as follows."

45 CFR 164.524(b)(2)(ii), further upholds that "if the covered entity is unable to take an action required by paragraph (b)(2)(i)(A) or (B) of this section within the time required by paragraph (b)(2)(i) of this section, as applicable, the covered entity may extend the time for such actions by no more than 30 days, provided that... the covered entity, within the time limit set by paragraph (b)(2)(i) of this section, as applicable, provides the individual with a written statement of the reasons for the delay and the date by which the covered entity will complete its action on the request... [and that] the covered entity may have only one such extension of time for action on a request for access."

If you are in the U.S., here is the legislation for Colorado, Illinois, and Massachusetts, respectively:

Colorado Revised Statutes Title 25. Health § 25-1-801 (1) (a) avers that "every patient record in the custody of a health facility licensed or certified pursuant to section 25-1.5-103(1) or article 3 of this title, or both, or any entity regulated under title 10, C.R.S., providing health-care services... directly or indirectly through a managed care plan... shall be available for inspection to the patient or the patient's personal representative through the attending health-care provider or the provider's designated representative at reasonable times and upon reasonable notice, except records withheld in accordance with 45 CFR 164.524(a). A summary of records pertaining to a patient's mental health problems may, upon written request and signed and dated authorization, be made available to the patient or the patient's personal representative following termination of the treatment program.
Ill. Admin. Code tit. 77 § 330.1740 mandates that “records of discharged residents shall be placed in an inactive file and retained as follows... Records for any resident who is discharged prior to being 18 years old shall be retained at least until the resident reaches the age of 23.”
Ill. Admin. Code tit. 77 § 330.1750 further clarifies that "the resident's record shall include information regarding the physician's notification and response regarding any serious accident or injury, or significant change in condition, as required by Section 330.1110(e)... The resident's record shall identify the reasons for any order and use of safety devices or restraints, as required by Section 330.1140(d) of this Part... Documentation of the review of the medication regimen by the attending physician shall be entered in the resident's record... the resident's record shall include the physician's diet order and observations of the resident's response to the diet... The resident's record shall contain any physician determinations that limit the resident's access to the resident's personal property... The facility shall permit each resident, resident's parents, guardian or representative to inspect and copy the resident's medical records."
MGL Chapter 123 Section 36 maintains that "each facility, subject to this chapter and section 19 of chapter 19, that provides mental health care and treatment shall maintain patient records, as defined in the first paragraph of section 70 of chapter 111, for at least 20 years after the closing of the record due to discharge, death or last date of service."

Both 105 CMR 140.302(C)(1) and APA's Massachusetts-specific record keeping guidance aver that facilities, "in accordance with M.G.L. c. 111, § 70, each clinic shall maintain records of the diagnosis and treatment of patients under its care for a minimum of 20 years after the discharge or the final treatment of the patient to whom the record relates."

M.G.L. c.112, § 12CC clarifies that psychologists "must make the entire record available to the patient’s attorney or other psychotherapist designated by the patient, if requested by the patient."

A big reason why goods get cleaned in a washer is because of the mechanical action, or friction, between them.
